Excellencies, distinguished representatives, colleagues, I hereby declare open the third meeting of the 63rd session of the Human Rights Council. We will now continue the interactive dialogue with the Special Rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Afghanistan. We return to the list of speakers for national human rights institutions and non-governmental organizations, and I give the floor to the representative of Humanists International for a video intervention.

Thank you, Mr. President, and we thank the Special Rapporteur for this important report. I make this statement on behalf of Humanists International and the organizations co-sponsoring it, all of them endorsers of the Declaration on Gender Apartheid and its Destructive Consequences, launched in August. The declaration is also endorsed by Afghan-led organizations, including AISS and WCRAN. In this vein, we welcome the Special Rapporteur's reiteration of his recommendation to codify gender apartheid as a crime against humanity. That call has also been made by the UN Secretary-General and the High Commissioner, and by international legal and human rights experts from around the world who issued the declaration. In Afghanistan, we see religion and culture instrumentalized by the Taliban to justify the legal framework for gender apartheid, such as the law on the prevention of virtue and vice, and the recently enacted code on judicial separation of spouses. Such legal changes have validated child marriage and violence against women under a high threshold, as well as creating nearly insurmountable barriers to divorce for women. These laws and the proffered justifications for them all violate international law. Additionally, the declaration calls for the presumption of refugee status to be applied to women and girls fleeing gender apartheid. This is notable as we see states engaging with the de facto authorities in Afghanistan to facilitate deportations. We thank the Special Rapporteur for reminding states that they must comply with the non-derogable principle of non-refoulement. We ask the Special Rapporteur what must be done for the international community to heed the calls contained in the declaration, including to codify gender apartheid as a crime against humanity. Thank you.
Thank you. And I now give the floor to the representative of Human Rights Research League for a video intervention.

Thank you, Mr. President. More than five years after the Taliban's seizure of power, the humanitarian and human rights

situation in Afghanistan remains dire, and we thank Mr. Bennett for his thorough report. Hunger is widespread, with more than a third of the population facing acute food insecurity, including 9 million children.

This urgent situation had also been further aggravated by mass deportations conducted by Iran and Pakistan, often in violation

of the fundamental legal principle of non-refoulement, bringing the number of Afghan returnees from these two countries to close to 3 million in 2025 alone. It is against this backdrop that we need to contemplate the mental health situation in the country. Our recent research on mental health in times of war presented at this Council

demonstrated the devastating negative impact long-term war and crisis has on a country's population.

If we add to that the plight of women largely excluded from work and public life, and of girls excluded from education beyond sixth grade, it is evident that their loss of hope further

exacerbates the mental health situation of this particularly vulnerable group.

We therefore reiterate our call to States to refrain from normalizing relations with the de facto authorities unless and until significant demonstrable improvements in the human rights situation have been achieved. I thank you.
Thank you, and I now give the floor to the representative of the World Organization Against Torture.

Thank you, Mr. President. In every color, a story. In every melody, a memory. In every creation, a piece of identity. In every artist, a dream of freedom. Last month, de facto authorities adopted a new police law completely prohibiting demonstrations, further shrinking Afghanistan's already restricted civic space. At the same time, growing restrictions on music, artistic expression, and cultural activities are threatening Afghanistan's cultural diversity and heritage, while restricting fundamental rights and freedom. Artists, musicians, writers, filmmakers, and other cultural actors are increasingly unable to express themselves when their work is perceived as contrary to the Taliban's ideology. Mr. President, we refuse to be silenced. We resist because the soul of art is free. It cannot be confined, controlled, or erased. We therefore ask this Council to protect peaceful assembly, cultural rights, and freedom of expression, and to ensure that artists, journalists, human rights defenders, and civil society actors remain at the center of international engagement and accountability. Afghanistan blooms. Art resists. Hope remains. Thank you, Mr. President.

President, we welcome the SRS report. We call for an accelerated operationalization of the mechanism on Afghanistan and for ISIT to ensure that it has adequate financial support. fails to criminalize acts of physical violence against women by their

husbands unless they result in broken bones, wounds, and bruises, and it states that those who hold beliefs contrary to Sunni Islam are heretics. further entrenching discrimination against minority. Mr. President, Excellencies, As we approach the two-year anniversary of the fall of the former government, Syria continues to undergo a significant transformation, despite immense challenges. As many of you know, the People's Assembly was established, opening prospects for an independent and representative legislature, which we have welcomed. Millions of Syrians have returned home as reconstruction has accelerated. Integration efforts are also advancing significantly with the Syrian Democratic Forces announcing its dissolution and the completion and advancement of the integration process within state forces. We commend as commissioners, Commissioner Amara and I, these and many other achievements. but we are also mindful of the challenges inherent in building a legislature and a legitimate and accountable institution while addressing the legacy of atrocities and ensuring non-recurrence. In this regard, we commissioners and our team are extremely grateful for the renewal of the commission's core investigative mandate. The Commission has conducted regular missions to Syria, and both Commissioners have been there many times, including to Damascus, rural Damascus, Quneitra, Daraa, Sweida, Aleppo, Homs, Raqqa, and Hasaka since March alone. And we thank the government sincerely for ensuring continued access. In line with newly mandated tasks under our resolution, the Commission has also strengthened its engagement with authorities. We provide advice and follow-up on our recommendations from previous reports, and we also, in the months ahead, will be issuing policy papers that contain expert advice on core human rights issues, enabling and supporting the ongoing transition. The Commission also continues its very close engagement with victims and with witnesses, as well as with civil society, and we underscore how essential their continued role remains. Mr. President, ahead of our next report, next, uh, session, we would like to update this esteemed council on several key issues. First, the commission is deeply alarmed about continued Israeli violations. The Commission, including Commissioners, visited Quneitra and Daraa recently to meet with impacted communities who continue to report their bewilderment at Israeli actions while Syrians are rebuilding their country. Israeli military activity in south Syria is increasingly sustained and entrenched, with recurring ground incursions, patrols, raids, and searches. The establishment by Israel of a network of temporary checkpoints points, and fixed military infrastructure on Syrian territory has significantly affected civilians. Israel has also interrogated and detained hundreds of residents, Syrians, including minors. As of June 2026, the Commission has identified 49 individuals, including two children, detained by the IDF on Syrian territory, presumably rendered across Syrian borders. Such acts may amount to war crimes. The Commission is concerned that Israel's belligerent occupation has expanded its presence further and concurs with the Secretary-General's position, quote, "Violations of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity are unacceptable and must cease," end quote. Second, cognizant that accountability is a central component of successful transitional justice process, the Commission has stressed in its engagement with authorities the importance of ensuring that all perpetrators of violations are equally, underscore, the subject of accountability. The Commission warns that selective accountability breaches international legal obligations, could renew grievances, and undermine reconciliation. We stress that the centrality of due process and fair trial guarantees in judicial proceedings remains absolutely vital. We urge the government to ensure that the legality of detention of thousands of detained persons for alleged links to the Assad-era security institutions are addressed. Third, the commission acknowledges efforts by the government to address issues related to the March and July 2025 violence in the coast and Sweida. However, core human rights issues remain unresolved, fueling insecurity in Suweida. This includes the displacement of thousands of Druze and Bedouin families, the fate of the missing and the detained, and the ability of thousands of young students to sit their examinations. The lack of progress in addressing these issues is due to a continued standoff between local authorities and the national government, and that is compounded by continued interference by Israel in Syria. Notwithstanding that there have been a limited number of trials, accountability for violations that occurred in Soueida remains urgent and outstanding. Local authorities in Soueida should also refrain from further violations, including restrictions on movement and expression. Accountability for the violence in March 2025 also remains limited. Localised sectarian abuses and intimidation of the Alawite community persists. The Commission is also investigating reported killings predominantly targeting the Alawite community in Homs. Alleged abductions of women and girls in several governorates are also under investigation. We urge and stress that the government must ensure adequate gender-sensitive investigations and address the distress and the fear felt by certain communities. Fourth, the Commission has continued to investigate reported deaths in detention. and we've identified nine cases this year, and we were particularly troubled by the death of a former humanitarian worker in detention. We are, as commissioners and as commission staff, deeply cognizant of the challenges in eliminating these practices. We have documented them for years, and we know how challenging, given that past documentation, that work is, and we welcome statements that pledge accountability, and we look forward to engaging with the authorities to support robust and sustainable steps to eliminate torture. While freedoms have expanded considerably, the Commission engages authorities to increase further safeguards on many rights. In several cases, we note that activists have been arrested after criticising the government, and meanwhile, hate speech, often directed against certain groups, perceived on their alleged basis with the former government. We are particularly alarmed by the reports of threats of violence against women activists, including online. Further efforts are needed by all actors to counter hate speech while respecting freedom of expression. Lastly, the Commission has noted the government's meaningful efforts to mitigate violations during its operations in Aleppo and the northeast this year. Nevertheless, we are investigating reported violations, including the killing of civilians and Or de Combat fighters. Additionally, hundreds of SDF-aligned fighters remain missing. The Commission deplores previous child recruitment, which we have addressed on many occasions, and some of the fighters killed were reportedly underage. The situation of women and children who allegedly have ties to Daesh must be urgently resolved. It is absolutely deplorable that over 2,000 family members, mostly women and children, remain detained in Raj camp in northeast Syria. This constitutes the largest mass arbitrary detention site for women and children on security grounds anywhere in the world. And, as the Commission reports here today, conditions in the camp have worsened further. Additionally, more than 100 foreign children are arbitrarily held in military detention. We urge all States whose nationals are detained in that camp to support repatriation and rehabilitation without further delay. Earlier this year, more than 5,700 men and boys were forcibly transferred to Iraq in a rushed operation conducted by the United States without due process. This mass transfer may constitute a violation of the principle of non-refoulement on a massive scale and is under investigation by this Commission. Mr. President. The momentum to increase and cement respect for human rights in Syria remains high and must be supported by this Council and by the international community, not just in words, but in action. Concrete action must be taken to compel Israel to cease violations of rights of Syrians on Syrian territory. By breaking with the legacies of past violations and past violence, and putting in place solid foundations to prevent recurrence, Syria and the Syrian people can fulfill its aspirations for a human rights and dignity bearing society. The Commission, Commissioner Ammar and I, and our entire team remain committed to accompanying this transition positively and supporting efforts to ensure that the rights of the Syrian people are equally protected. Thank you very much.

The transitional justice council has prepared a draft transitional programme and reaffirmed the importance of the participation of victims. pursuing its investigations and remaining close to the victims to collect evidence. We drew inspiration from a constitutional declaration and new legislation that led to verdicts being handed down to perpetrators of violations. There were five complaints submitted, as well as 12 and 69 files that were submitted. There are 1,147 under investigation and 1,333 are before the Office of the Prosecutor. So Syria is determined to move from a stage of indifference and denial when it comes to violations to a new stage. That stage is based on shouldering responsibility and ensuring justice. We should also point out that the judiciary in Syria is committed to the principle of justice and this has been reaffirmed by international fora, while respecting judicial safeguards and procedures which respect assumed commitments. This is a new legislative process that has been approved by the instance representing the Syrian people, the National Missing Persons Commission, is has the mandate regarding missing persons. It has launched a debate, a broad consultation in which victims had a voice. It also opened counselling centres and launched a programme to enable witness testimony to be collected regarding missing persons. There have been 194 cases initiated, some of which have been initiated in co-operation with international fora that have a similar mandate. The Syrian Government has also drafted a national strategy to fight torture and to find a settlement regarding proven cases of torture committed during the defunct regime. We also opened the voice to correspondence for them to investigate in that respect. While Syria is committed to the path of stability and international cooperation, it continues to prosecute violations committed against civilians in gross violation of international law and complete inference to the line of disengagement line of 1974. That is why we call on Israel to cease its violations and to release civilians who have been detained by it. We continue to face major challenges, especially when it comes to accountability, collection of evidence and ensuring justice to the victims. We welcome the establishment of an early warning system. We reaffirm that we are committed to pursuing our co-operation. It is the common denominator to ensure justice and to co-operate when it comes to collecting information, while recognising the right of victims and witnesses to unanimity. Thank you. Excellencies, distinguished representatives, colleagues. We will now hear the oral update by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights on the human rights situation in and around El Obeid in the context of the ongoing conflict in the Sudan, pursuant to Council resolution 62/1. We will also hear the presentation of the written update by the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights on promoting reconciliation, accountability and human rights in Sri Lanka, pursuant to Council resolution 51/1. I now have the honor to give the floor to Ms. Awad Abou, the Deputy High Commissioner for Human Rights, to present the updates. Madame, you have the floor.

Thank you. Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, on the 3rd of July, this Council met to urge immediate action to protect civilians in light of the deteriorating situation in El Obeid in North Kordofan State. Since then, there have been signs that international pressure has helped to make a difference on the ground. Drone strikes in El Obeid city decreased sharply in July, offering some relief to civilians who had endured months of fear and deprivation. However, civilians in El Obeid are still living in dire conditions and face grave risks. Repeated drone strikes on gas stations, on water, electricity infrastructure have left families struggling to access safe water, food, and medical care as prices soar. In the past six months of 2026, our office documented at least 1,120 civilian deaths as a result of drone strikes across Sudan. accounting for 80% of all civilian deaths that we documented. The Kordofan region remains the current epicenter of the conflict in Sudan. The majority of civilian deaths documented by our office to date in 2026 were recorded in this region. Hostilities have intensified in areas to the north of El Obeid, as the Sudan Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces have battled for control over key supply routes linking North Kordofan to Khartoum and Darfur. In August, ground hostilities resumed to the south and west of El Obeid, restricting access to a key water source for the city. People fleeing intensified fighting are also moving towards El Obeid, straining limited resources and, in some cases, fuelling mistrust towards new arrivals. In South Kordofan, clashes between the RSF-affiliated Sudan's People's Liberation Movement-North and the Otoro community in Kauda have led to casualties and displacement. We are deeply concerned about ongoing attacks on humanitarian personnel and assets. This includes the detention of humanitarian workers by the SPLM-North, the looting of a warehouse in Kauda, and the aerial strike outside Dilling that destroyed World Food Programme trucks carrying aid. We also sound the alarm about the sharp increase in hostilities in Blue Nile State, as the RSF and SPLM-North announced the capture of Kourtouk and Gaysan along the border with Ethiopia. In North Darfur, RSF ground incursions and drone activity in the Dar Zaghawa area have triggered further displacement. As civilians flee conflict and insecurity, they continue to face summary killings, sexual violence, other physical violence, arbitrary detention, abductions, and looting. Tensions between communities are deepening, fueling hate speech. In some areas, the defection of RSF commanders and shifting alliances are fueling intercommunal violence. The High Commissioner's designated expert discussed a proposal for confidence-building measures with the authorities just last week, and we hope this dialogue will contribute to meaningful measures to protect civilians. Mr. President, this horrific war has been fueled by interests, both inside and outside the country. Yesterday, the Independent Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan briefed this Council on its findings that foreign powers and entities have supplied weapons and other military support. Meanwhile, as our own report earlier this year set out, Domestic and external players are exploiting the country's rich natural resources, from gold to gum arabic. The ultimate price is being paid by the Sudanese people. The international community must act to end the transfer of arms to the parties used in manifest disregard of the obligation to protect civilians. And as long as perpetrators of human rights violations face no consequences, the violence will continue. States need to use every available tool to ensure justice for victims, including through universal jurisdiction, and to fully support the International Criminal Court's mandate with respect to accountability for crimes committed in Darfur. And finally, sustained international efforts are needed to secure a permanent ceasefire and to support a transition to inclusive civilian rule. The people of Sudan need protection, justice, and sustainable peace. Thank you. Mr. President, Your Excellencies, I now turn to update on Sri Lanka. A year ago, following his visit to the country, the High Commissioner highlighted that the recently elected government had a mandate for clear and transformative reforms to help Sri Lanka heal from cycles of violence, impunity, and inequality. A month later, this Council's resolution 60/1 call for concrete steps towards reconciliation, accountability, and advancing human rights in Sri Lanka. Since then, there have been some important steps towards investigation and prosecution in a few emblematic cases of alleged political killings and enforced disappearances. Last month, indictments were filed against a former politician and others regarding the 20 the 2006 murder of the Vice Chancellor of Eastern University. A former intelligence chief has been arrested, and a former police chief and a senior defense official have been convicted in connection with the Easter Sunday bombings. The government has taken steps to tackle corruption, and we welcome the recent ratification of the International Labor Organization Convention on freedom from violence and harassment in the workplace, including gender-based abuses. The president has repeatedly denounced racism and sectarianism, sectarian politics, emphasizing national unity in the face of a series of external shocks, including the devastating cyclone of November 2025 and the global spike in energy costs. However, the promise of deeper legal institutional reforms appears to be stalling. There has been no progress towards broader recognition and accountability for crimes under international law and gross violations committed by the state security forces or the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam during decades of armed conflict. There is continued intimidation of victims and witnesses, and efforts to protect them are clearly inadequate. Even where serious violations have been well documented, many criminal investigations remain endlessly delayed. The government has not yet fulfilled its commitment to establish an independent public prosecutor operating separately from the Attorney General's Department. Meaningful security sector reform is still absent. Personnel suspected of serious violations continue to operate within the military and police forces, and there are frequent reports of torture and deaths in custody. The government continues to rely on the repressive Prevention of Terrorism Act The draft law on the protection of the state from terrorism retains many provisions that pose a risk to fundamental freedoms, including due process and fair trial guarantees and effective judicial oversight. Human rights defenders and victims still face surveillance and intimidation by state intelligence services, particularly in the northern and eastern Sri Lanka. A draft proposal on the registration and supervision of non-governmental organizations raises serious concerns about disproportionate and overbroad executive powers, excessive and burdensome requirements, and the restrictions on civil society groups on autonomy, independence, and access to funding. Although several mass grave sites have been reopened, there is little public confidence in the Office of Missing Persons. It recently reported that it has resolved 32 cases, but the fate and whereabouts of tens and thousands of disappeared people remains unknown. Reforms are badly needed to ensure the office's independence and capacity, the protection of witnesses, and full cooperation from state agencies and security forces. It is also unfortunate that the government has rejected our findings and recommendations, to advance accountability for conflict-related sexual violence. Mr. President, the Sri Lankan authorities undoubtedly face very serious constraints, beginning with a crushing burden of debt. Some 82% of government revenue in the 2026 budget is allocated to interest and repayment of public loans, more than double the total spent on health, education, and social protection. This is a crucial human rights issue. The country urgently needs more development support, including for post-cyclone reconstruction, with particular focus on the Malayala Tamil community and others in vulnerable situations. More broadly, it is vital that the momentum for change, which swept the country two years ago, is not lost. Our office is eager to assist Sri Lanka in advancing legal and institutional reforms including initiatives to ensure genuine accountability, justice, and countrywide reconciliation. Those responsible for serious crimes must face prosecution, including through the application of extraterritorial or universal jurisdiction or other international avenues. close screening of security forces personnel is needed, including for peacekeeping and other international operations. Continued engagement by this Council will be vital to advancing accountability, national reconciliation and sustainable peace. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. President. Sri Lanka takes note of the written update of the Office of the High Commissioner. Sri Lanka has constantly engaged with this Council and UN human rights mechanisms in the spirit of transparency and cooperation, while maintaining that sustainable progress in human rights and reconciliation must be nationally owned, nationally driven, and responsive to domestic realities. Mr. President, this month marks two years since President Ranil Kumaratne was selected with a mandate for economic, social and political transformation. Despite significant challenges, including Cyclone Dikda and global uncertainties, the Government has made considerable progress towards building a just, fair and prosperous society. Returning to upper-middle income status, Sri Lanka recorded 5% real GDP growth in 2025. Strong anti-corruption drive continues, including strengthening the commission to investigate allegations of bribery or corruption and the National Anti-Corruption Action Plan 2025-2029. Mr. President, Sri Lanka did not support resolution 6/1, including provisions extending the mandate of the external evidence gathering mechanism. Such external mechanisms risk creating divisions and undermining genuine national processes already in place. We note the OHCHR's recognition of positive developments, including progress in investigations, anti-corruption measures, reconciliation and memorialization. In the past year, the Government steadfastly pursued an agenda for reforms promoting reconciliation and human rights. If I may mention a few, following consultations with UN and international partners, The Prevention of Terrorism Act is to be repealed and replaced by a new legislation that guarantees fundamental freedoms and prevents abuse. The draft law is being gestated and will be presented to Parliament in the coming month. Stakeholder consultations on amendments to Online Safety Act have been completed and the amendments are being finalised. Independent reconciliation mechanisms, such as Office for Missing Persons, Office for Reparations, and Office for National Unity and Reconciliation, continue to fulfill their mandates with strengthened resources. The existing draft framework of a Truth and Reconciliation Commission is being reviewed to avoid overlaps with mandates of other reconciliation mechanisms. A committee headed by a Supreme Court judge continues to study proposals to establish an independent prosecutor's office. Inter-Ministerial Committee has been appointed by the Cabinet to examine issues concerning land release, valuation and compensation. The Cabinet has approved special immigration measures to facilitate voluntary and safe return of Sri Lankan refugees in India who left during the conflict without valid travel documents. For the first time, the Government is addressing long-standing concerns of the Malayala community expeditiously and comprehensively. The Government remains committed to ensuring that any alleged unlawful act is investigated and prosecuted through an independent national process, regardless of social status or background. Recent action in several high-profile cases, including reopened investigations, demonstrates this commitment. As acknowledged in the High Commissioner's written update, the Government remains committed to the pledge given by the President that there will be no room for a resurgence of racism or extremism in Sri Lanka. The Government remains committed to safeguarding judicial independence, separation of powers and access to justice. Proposed legal reforms to increase the number of judges and the retirement age of all judges aim to strengthen the capacity and efficiency of the justice system, address case backlogs and delays, retain judicial expertise and institutional knowledge, and enhancing access to justice and facilitating appellate jurisdiction at regional level. We recognize the challenges within our prison system. The government is taking accelerated measures to improve prison administration, reduce overcrowding, and strengthen rehabilitation. A committee of inquiry is investigating recent events at Negombo Prison. Mr. President, Sri Lanka has traveled a long and challenging road. The end of conflict marked not the end of challenges, but the beginning of a long process of healing, rebuilding and reconciliation. That process requires recognition of progress, understanding and encouragement. And the government remains steadfast in delivering its commitment. In conclusion, we respectfully urge that Sri Lanka's situation be assessed in a balanced, objective and constructive manner in keeping with the principles governing this Council, and that Sri Lanka be supported in its national efforts towards a just, prosperous and reconciled nation. Thank you very much.

Thank you, President. I deliver this statement on behalf of MIKTA, Mexico, Indonesia, the Republic of Korea, Turkey, and Australia.
